title: Alien Dictionary
statement: You are given a list of words from an alien language, sorted lexicographically by that language's unknown alphabet order. Derive a string of the distinct letters in an order consistent with the given sorting, or return "" if no such order exists.
realWorld: Recovering an implicit ordering from observed sorted output — the same shape as inferring a schema's column order from sorted exports, or reconstructing a version precedence from a sorted release list.

examples.explanation: wrt < wrf gives t < f. wrf < er gives w < e. er < ett gives r < t. ett < rftt gives e < r. Chain them: w < e < r < t < f.
z < x and x < z. The constraints contradict each other, so no alphabet can produce this sorting.
The invalid-prefix case. A prefix always sorts before the longer word in any alphabet, so a longer word appearing before its own prefix is impossible regardless of letter order.

constraints: words[i] consists of lowercase English letters
Only letters that actually appear in the input belong in the output

bruteForce.idea: Generate every permutation of the distinct letters and keep the first one under which the given word list is correctly sorted.

complexity.time: O(k! * n * L) for k distinct letters, n words of length L

bruteForce.whySlow: With all 26 letters present there are 26! permutations — about 4 x 10^26. And the check throws away the useful information: comparing two adjacent words tells you one concrete ordering fact, which the permutation search rediscovers from scratch every time.

patternIdentification: Two things have to click. First, each adjacent pair of words yields at most one ordering constraint — the first position where they differ, and nothing after it (everything past the first difference is already decided by that difference). Second, 'letter x must come before letter y' over a set of letters is a directed graph, and 'produce a full ordering consistent with all constraints' is a topological sort. The contradiction case ('z' before 'x' and 'x' before 'z') becomes a cycle, which Kahn's algorithm reports for free.

optimized.idea: Build a graph over the distinct letters. For each adjacent word pair, scan to the first differing character and add that single edge; if no character differs but the first word is longer, the input is invalid. Then run Kahn's algorithm. Use a Set for the adjacency so a repeated constraint does not inflate an indegree twice. A short output means a cycle, so the constraints contradict.

complexity.time: O(C + k) where C is the total number of characters in the input and k the number of distinct letters
complexity.space: O(k) — at most 26 nodes and 26*25 edges, so effectively O(1)

commonMistakes: Adding an edge for every differing position instead of only the first. Everything after the first difference is unconstrained — 'abc' < 'abd' says nothing about c versus anything beyond d.
Missing the invalid-prefix case. ["abc","ab"] must return "", and checking only the shared prefix positions silently accepts it.
Omitting letters that appear in no constraint. Every distinct letter must be in the output, so seed the node set from the words, not from the edges.
Using a List for the adjacency, so a constraint repeated by two different word pairs increments the indegree twice and nothing ever reaches zero.
Comparing against one expected string. Several alphabets can be consistent with the input when constraints are incomplete; verify against the constraints instead.
Treating the cycle case as an error to throw. Contradictory constraints are a legitimate input whose answer is "".
